title: The student who asked about om
hookLine: Satyakama asks what a life of om leads to; a, u, m hold waking, dream and deep sleep
carry: a, u, m: waking, dream, deep sleep
tomorrow: The teacher who answered with silence

cards: Six seekers once came to a sage named Pippalada, firewood in hand. He told them: live here a year first, with discipline and faith. Then ask anything.

One of them, Satyakama, asked what any chanting family might ask. Sir, if someone meditates on om all their life, to the very end, where does it lead? Pippalada said: om is Brahman, both the higher and the lower.
Hold one part of it, and you go part of the way. Hold all three of its sounds together, and you reach the highest.

teach.b: Three sounds? The Mandukya spells them out. Verse eight: this self, as a syllable, is om.

The quarters are the letters, and the letters are the quarters: a, u, m. In Sanskrit the o of om is a and u blended, which is why it's also written aum. Verse nine: waking is a, the first sound, the open mouth.

teach.h: A WAKING, U DREAM, M SLEEP.
teach.b: Verse ten: dream is u, the rounding lips, in between, the way dream sits between waking and sleep.
Verse eleven: deep sleep is m, the lips closing, where the sound gathers, the way waking and dream fold into sleep each night.
The text backs each link with wordplay, a sound suggesting a meaning, the kind the Upanishads use often.

teach.h: SAY IT SLOWLY: AH, OO, MMM.
teach.b: So say it slowly: ah, oo, mmm. Back of the throat, to the lips, closed. One breath walks through a whole day and night.
And the fourth? It has no letter. That's tomorrow.
This is why om comes first in so many Hindu mantras: om namah shivaya, om namo narayanaya.

Before you ask for anything, you name all of it: everything you're awake to, everything you dream, everything you rest in. Some families say a quiet om before a long drive or an exam for the same reason.
Today, most days are lived in pieces: the morning rush, the scrolling half-dream, the crash at night. Om is the Hindu way of holding the whole day in one breath, and offering it.

how: Hindu teachers who follow the Mandukya instruct students to chant om as three sounds, a-u-m, followed by silence, following the Mandukya's mapping of the letters to waking, dream and deep sleep.

o: a grammar book on how to spell in Sanskrit
a songbook of chants for temple festivals
an Upanishad that maps a, u, m onto three states

games.q: om, letter by letter — tap the pairs.

s: Pippalada answered the seekers the day they arrived
he asked them to live with him a year first, then ask anything.
the Mandukya gives the fourth its own letter
a, u and m are the first three quarters; the fourth has no letter.
dream is linked to u because it sits between waking and deep sleep
the way u sits between a and m.

games.q: you're mapping the three sounds of om onto the three states. which sound goes with deep sleep?
games.why: m: the lips close, the sound gathers, and waking and dream merge into deep sleep.

practice: If you're comfortable, chant om slowly three times, out loud or silently, feeling each sound in your mouth: on the ah, think waking; on the oo, dream; on the mmm, deep sleep. After the third, stay in the silence and add nothing.
If chanting isn't your practice, simply breathe in three parts and rest after each out-breath.

wordCard.voice: The Mandukya Upanishad. Om, letter by letter: a is waking, u is dream, m is deep sleep. The fourth has no letter.

orig.note: Sanskrit: matra, measure, element, a letter's unit of sound; Mandukya 8: the quarters are the matras, a, u, m.

carryVoice: Your line: a, u, m: waking, dream, deep sleep. A whole day and night in one syllable. That's day two hundred fifty-eight.

Mandukya Upanishad 8 (the quarters are the letters)
